name: Ramappa Temple (Rudreshwara), Palampet
summary: The UNESCO-listed Ramappa temple in Telangana is a masterpiece of Kakatiya art — a Shiva temple of 1213 CE on a star-shaped platform, unique in bearing the name of its sculptor, and famous for “floating” bricks and jewel-like basalt figures.

sections.history: The Rudreshwara temple at Palampet was consecrated in 1213 CE by Recharla Rudra, a general of the Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, in the era when the Kakatiyas ruled much of the Telugu country from Warangal. Almost uniquely among Indian temples, it is remembered by the name of its sculptor, Ramappa — a measure of the fame his artistry earned. Marco Polo is popularly said to have called it the brightest star in the galaxy of temples. In 2021 UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site, honouring both its beauty and its remarkable engineering.
sections.architecture: The temple stands on a high, star-shaped platform, built of reddish sandstone but crowned with a tower of “floating bricks” so light they are said to be able to float on water, lending the superstructure its slender rise. Against the warm stone gleam sculptures of black basalt, polished like metal: the madanikas and naginis — dancers and celestial women — that bracket the eaves are among the most celebrated figures in Indian art. A great Nandi faces the sanctum, and the whole rests, tradition and study agree, on a “sandbox” foundation that has helped it endure earthquakes for eight centuries.
sections.legends: The temple’s very name carries its legend: that a sculptor named Ramappa laboured so long and so brilliantly on this shrine that the temple came to bear his name rather than the god’s or the king’s — a rare honour in a tradition where craftsmen are usually anonymous. The dancing madanikas are woven into local lore for their lifelike grace, said to have been carved from living models, and pilgrims and travellers alike have marvelled for centuries that stone could be made to move so.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple’s principal festival, when devotees gather through the night before Rudreshwara. Kartika Masam, sacred to Shiva, brings lamps and special worship, and the temple shares in the Telangana festival calendar of the surrounding Kakatiya country. Since its UNESCO inscription, cultural programmes of classical dance and music are also staged here, fittingly celebrating the dancing figures carved into its very eaves.
sections.experience: Approached across the fields of Palampet, the Ramappa temple rewards a slow, close look. The eye is drawn upward to the black basalt bracket-figures — dancers caught mid-movement, so finely cut that anklets and ornaments seem to tremble — and then out over the great Nandi and the star-shaped platform. The setting is rural and calm, a lake nearby, and the temple’s survival through eight centuries of earthquakes lends every detail an added wonder. Early light or late afternoon brings out the contrast of warm sandstone and gleaming dark sculpture.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 6:00 am to 6:00 pm daily; as a protected monument and living temple, worship and visiting hours may vary on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is appreciated, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed of the exterior and sculptures; follow any posted rules within the sanctum and during worship.
visit.gettingThere: Palampet is in Mulugu district, about 70 km from Warangal and 200 km from Hyderabad; the temple is reached by road, with Warangal the nearest major rail junction and Hyderabad the nearest airport.
